M2-01-NORMALIZZAZIONE.4:
## The EBITDA you negotiate on is almost never the EBITDA in the accounts

EBITDA "as reported" in the accounts is rarely the business's true EBITDA: it contains costs and income that won't happen again, or that don't reflect normal market conditions. A Quality of Earnings (QoE) review adjusts them to reach a **normalised** (or *adjusted*) EBITDA — the one a multiple is really negotiated on. The general formula, which you'll reuse throughout this module, is:

> **Normalised EBITDA = Reported EBITDA + Σ adjustments**

Every adjustment has a precise sign, and getting it wrong is the most common beginner's mistake:

- a one-off or off-market **cost**, already inside reported EBITDA, INFLATED costs (and so DEFLATED reported EBITDA): it's ADDED BACK, a **positive** adjustment.
- a one-off **revenue/income** item, already inside reported EBITDA, INFLATED reported EBITDA: it's REMOVED, a **negative** adjustment.

Here you have a single case, the simplest: reported EBITDA is {p0}, and it includes {p1} of exceptional legal fees for a concluded lawsuit — a cost that won't recur in future years. It's an adjustment to add back.

Once you've calculated normalised EBITDA, also look at how big the adjustment is in proportion: if total adjustments exceed 15-20% of reported EBITDA, a buyer starts wondering how clean the business really is — and how much the "adjusted" EBITDA has been artfully inflated.

M2-02-COMPENSOAMMINISTRATORE.6:
## A related-party adjustment can go either way

The compensation paid to the director/owner is the first item a QoE checks: it's a related-party expense, decided by whoever controls the company, not by the market. The comparison is always with **market compensation**: what it would cost to hire an outside manager for the same role.

The adjustment ALWAYS has the same formula — compensation paid minus market compensation — but the SIGN of the result depends on who is under- or overpaid, and must be understood before writing it:

- if compensation paid is ABOVE market, the overpayment inflated costs (and so deflated reported EBITDA): it's ADDED BACK, a **positive** adjustment.
- if compensation paid is BELOW market, labour cost is understated and INFLATED reported EBITDA: a buyer will have to pay a real manager at market rates, so EBITDA must be REDUCED. A **negative** adjustment — the less intuitive case, typical of family businesses where the founder underpays themselves, but just as real as the first.

This company's reported EBITDA is {p0}. {spiegazioneCaso}

M2-02-COMPENSOAMMINISTRATORE.16: ={B_EBITDA_RIP}+{B_RETTIFICA}: reported EBITDA plus the adjustment already calculated, with its sign. If the adjustment is negative, adding it subtracts automatically.

M2-03-AFFITTIINFRAGRUPPO.4:
## Rent paid to the owning family

The company doesn't own the building it operates from: it rents it from a property company belonging to the same owning family — a related party. When whoever receives the rent and whoever pays it answer to the same people, the price paid isn't guaranteed to be a market price: it may have been set to shift value from one entity to the other, not to reflect what renting that property from an independent third party would really cost.

Here reported EBITDA is {p0}. The company pays {p1} a year in rent to the related party; a market rent for an equivalent property in the same area — estimated from an independent benchmark — would be {p2}. The difference is a premium the company pays only because the property owner is also the company's owner: an outside buyer, who would renegotiate the lease on market terms, wouldn't bear that extra cost.

As in every QoE adjustment, the sign follows the general rule: an off-market cost, already inside reported EBITDA, inflated costs (and so deflated reported EBITDA) — it's ADDED BACK, a **positive** adjustment.

M2-05-ONEOFFLEGALI.14:
## Not all legal expenses are equal

A list of legal and restructuring expenses almost always mixes two different things: the company's normal legal management (contracts, employment, collections — costs that come back every year) and exceptional episodes (a lawsuit, a restructuring plan — costs that won't recur). Only the second category is a matter for adjustment.

- **"recurring"** items are normal legal management: they're NOT touched.
- **"one-off"** items are exceptional, already inside reported EBITDA, and inflated it in costs (and so deflated EBITDA): they're ADDED BACK, a **positive** adjustment.

Adding up the whole list indiscriminately would be a conceptual error, not a detail: the total of ALL items is {p2}, but only part of that number is really exceptional. Isolate the right rows first, then add up.

M2-06-PLUSMINUSVALENZE.11:
## Asset disposal: the sign depends on gain or loss, not on the event itself

So far in this module you've always met **positive** adjustments: a one-off cost already inside reported EBITDA is added back. Here you meet the other side of the same rule:

> **Normalised EBITDA = Reported EBITDA + Σ adjustments**

- a one-off **cost** that inflated costs (deflated reported EBITDA) is ADDED BACK: a **positive** adjustment.
- a one-off **revenue/income** item that inflated reported EBITDA is REMOVED: a **negative** adjustment.

M2-07-CAPITALIZZAZIONEIMPROPRIA.2: In {B_RETTIFICA} compute the net adjustment, adding up TWO components that BOTH get removed from reported EBITDA (negative adjustment on both): the share improperly capitalised this year ({p1}, in {B_CAPITALIZZATO}) — a cost that should have hit the income statement in full and was instead recorded as an intangible asset, so it inflated reported EBITDA — and the one-off government grant ({p3}, in {B_CONTRIBUTO}), non-recurring income that inflated reported EBITDA in the same way. M2-07-CAPITALIZZAZIONEIMPROPRIA.4:
## Capitalising isn't always legitimate

In M1 you saw a company legitimately move part of its R&D spending from the income statement to the balance sheet, under verifiable OIC criteria: demonstrable technical feasibility, intention and ability to complete the project, reliable future economic benefits. Here the same accounting move — capitalising a cost instead of expensing it — was made WITHOUT any of these justifications: a cost that under the rules should have hit the income statement in full was instead recorded as an intangible asset. The cost hasn't disappeared, it's been hidden below the line — and reported EBITDA comes out artificially higher.

Below you'll find reported EBITDA ({p0}) and two items to adjust, both with the SAME sign:

- **improperly capitalised share** ({p1}): a cost that should have been entirely in the income statement and isn't — reported EBITDA is HIGHER than it should be. It's REMOVED: a **negative** adjustment.
- **one-off government grant** ({p2}): non-recurring income, received once and booked as operating income, which won't recur in future years. Like every one-off income item seen in this module, it inflated reported EBITDA: this gets REMOVED too. A **negative** adjustment.

**Careful**: the two adjustments have different reasons (one is a hidden cost, the other income that won't recur) but the SAME sign. Don't net them against each other: they both add up with a negative sign, and the net adjustment is bigger than either one on its own.

M2-08-EFFETTICAMBIO.4:
## An FX gain can hide inside a cost, not only in revenue

This company imports raw materials in foreign currency. Because of how it keeps its books — ITS OWN classification choice, not the general accounting standard — it books REALISED FX gains and losses on trade payables directly inside the cost of raw materials, instead of in financial items below EBITDA (where FX effects would normally sit, without touching EBITDA at all). Keep it in mind: it's not the general convention, it's a quirk of this company.

This year a strong currency move generated a **non-recurring FX gain** of {p0}, which ended up inside that cost — and so inside reported EBITDA of {p1}, inflating it.

The rule is always the same:

> **Normalised EBITDA = Reported EBITDA + Σ adjustments**

- a one-off **cost** that inflated costs (deflated reported EBITDA) is ADDED BACK: a **positive** adjustment.
- a one-off **revenue/income** item that inflated reported EBITDA is REMOVED: a **negative** adjustment.

An FX gain is income, not a cost — even if here it lives inside a cost line. In this level the adjustment is always negative: there's no "FX loss" case to compare, the point is to fix this single sign firmly before moving on in the module.

M2-09-RUNRATE.6:
## Run-rate: annualise only what has already happened

A serious QoE distinguishes two things that look alike but aren't the same:

- **Legitimate run-rate** — an action ALREADY TAKEN during the year (a site closed, a contract renegotiated). Its full effect already exists, at steady state: but only PART of it shows in reported EBITDA, because the action wasn't active from 1 January. Annualising it is legitimate: nothing is invented, you're just showing the true effect of a decision already made.
- **Aspirational pro-forma** — a saving HOPED FOR from a plan not yet approved. It hasn't happened yet, and may never happen: a serious QoE doesn't include it, in any form.

**The action.** This year the company completed {azioneLabel}, in {meseNome}. The cost saving generated is {p2} per MONTH (given directly: no need to derive it from an annual saving).

From {meseNome} (included) to year end {p3} months have elapsed: that's the part of the year in which the saving is ALREADY inside reported EBITDA of {p4}. The months BEFORE execution didn't benefit from the saving — that missing part is exactly what the run-rate adjustment must add.

**Careful, a trap figure.** Management has also indicated a hoped-for additional saving of {p5}, from an efficiency plan the board hasn't approved yet. It's not an action taken: it's a management aspiration. It does NOT go into any formula in this level — it's here on purpose so you learn to recognise it and discard it.

M2-10-LTM.2: In {B_LTM} compute LTM (Last Twelve Months) EBITDA: the last full fiscal year FY ({B_FY}) plus the current year's H1 ({B_H1_CORRENTE}) MINUS the same period of the previous year's H1 ({B_H1_PRECEDENTE}). The FY already includes those six months: if you don't remove them, you count them twice. Formula: FY + current H1 - previous H1.
M2-10-LTM.3: In {B_GIORNI} check that the LTM window really covers 12 months: subtract the previous H1 closing date ({B_DATA_PRECEDENTE}) from the current H1 closing date ({B_DATA_CORRENTE}). Use direct subtraction between the two date cells — no EDATE, EOMONTH or YEARFRAC here, subtraction is enough and safer. The result must be 365 or 366 (depending on whether a 29 February falls inside the window), never any other number: if it doesn't come out that way, the two starting dates don't really cover an exact year.
M2-10-LTM.4:
## LTM: twelve real months, not a doubling

A buyer never negotiates on the last closed annual accounts (they can contain up to 18 months of stale data) nor on a projection obtained by doubling the latest available half-year. They use **LTM** (*Last Twelve Months*): the last 12 ACTUALLY observed months, rebuilt by adding and subtracting pieces of accounts already published.

> **LTM EBITDA = FY (last full fiscal year) + current H1 − previous H1**

The most recent FY already includes, inside it, the six months of "previous H1" (the same period a year earlier, already closed within that FY). Adding the current H1 without removing the previous H1 would count those six months TWICE — the subtraction isn't a technical detail, it's what avoids double counting.

**Why isn't doubling the current H1 enough to estimate the year?** Because a seasonal business — retail with Black Friday and Christmas, tourism with summer — doesn't spread EBITDA evenly between the two halves. Here, for example, the current H1 is {p0}: doubling it would give {p1}, a number quite different from the true LTM (which you'll calculate). If the strong half of the year is the one NOT yet observed, doubling UNDERSTATES the year; if it's the one already past, it OVERSTATES it. LTM gets around the problem because it projects nothing: it only uses data that really happened.

**The data.** On {giornoChiusura}/{meseChiusura}/{annoPrecedente} the previous year's H1 closed, and FY {annoPrecedente} (the full fiscal year, already published) made {p5} of EBITDA. On {giornoChiusura}/{meseChiusura}/{annoCorrente} the current H1 closed, with EBITDA of {p7}. The same half of the previous year (already included in FY {annoPrecedente}) had made {p8}.

## An addback isn't an opinion: it's a documentable fact

A target's management almost always proposes more adjustments than a serious buyer will accept. Some are legitimate: a real one-off cost, with an invoice or minutes to prove it. Others SOUND legitimate but aren't — synergies not yet realised, a plan just approved and never executed, a recurring cost relabelled as exceptional to make it vanish from reported EBITDA.

Reported EBITDA is {p0}. Below you'll find {p1} adjustments proposed by management. For each one you decide, in the Valid column, whether it's defensible ("YES") or not ("NO"): it's in the description that you see the difference between a fact and a hope.

- Valid **"YES"**: there's concrete evidence behind it (invoice, minutes, settlement agreement). It's ADDED BACK, a positive adjustment.
- Valid **"NO"**: it's an estimate, an aspiration or an opportunistic reclassification. It's NOT touched — it doesn't go into the sum.

Adding up the whole list indiscriminately would be a conceptual error, not a detail: the total of ALL proposals is {p2}, but only part of that number is really defensible in front of a buyer.

A serious buyer rejects the adjustments you can't prove with a document: if you can't point to the evidence, it's not an addback, it's an opinion.

## The adjustment schedule: the module in one sheet

You've seen, one case at a time, how related-party items (director compensation, rents, the owner's personal costs), one-offs (legal fees, restructuring, gains/losses on disposal, FX effects, improper capitalisation) and aggressive management proposals adjust reported EBITDA. In a real QoE these categories don't arrive one at a time: they all arrive together, in a single mixed SCHEDULE you must learn to read row by row, without losing the sign discipline seen so far:

> **Normalised EBITDA = Reported EBITDA + Σ adjustments**

- a one-off or off-market **cost** that inflated costs (deflated reported EBITDA) is ADDED BACK: a **positive** adjustment.
- a one-off **revenue/income** item, or a cost hidden by improper capitalisation, that inflated reported EBITDA is REMOVED: a **negative** adjustment.

This year's reported EBITDA is {p0}. Below you'll find {p1} proposed adjustments, each with an amount ALREADY written with the correct sign for its category. One of them is a management proposal with no supporting documents: for each row you decide, in the Valid column, whether it's acceptable ("YES") or not ("NO").

Then look at the result in proportion: above 15-20% of reported EBITDA a buyer starts getting suspicious, even if every item is documented, and will put the multiple under pressure.
